answer: Reverse causation occurs when Y causes X rather than X causing Y, and a feedback loop arises when X and Y cause each other simultaneously. Correlation alone cannot distinguish these cases: a link between higher chronic disease rates and lower employment is equally consistent with illness reducing work capacity or job loss worsening health. When variables influence each other, the system settles into an equilibrium and standard regression cannot recover a causal effect. This CAPHE lab shows that the remedy is not more controls but exogenous variation that shifts one variable without coming from the other, identifying a single direction and a leverage point for intervention.

faqs.q: What is the difference between reverse causation and a feedback loop?
faqs.a: Reverse causation means the causal arrow points the opposite way from what was assumed, so Y causes X. A feedback loop means X causes Y and Y causes X at the same time, so small changes amplify and the variables settle into an equilibrium.

faqs.q: Why can't adding more control variables fix reverse causation?
faqs.a: Controls address omitted confounders, not the direction of causation. When two variables influence each other, regression cannot tell which way the effect runs. Identification requires exogenous variation that moves one variable without coming from the other.

faqs.q: How do economists find leverage points in a feedback system?
faqs.a: They look for an external shock, such as a policy change or natural experiment, that affects only one side of the loop. That exogenous variation isolates one direction of causation and reveals where intervention yields the largest equilibrium shift per dollar.

faqs.q: Can timing help separate cause from effect in feedback loops?
faqs.a: Yes. If X takes years to affect Y while Y affects X quickly, panel data with enough periods can exploit those lags to identify one direction of causation at a time.
